planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; Vanguard is one of the very earliest tommasinianus crocus to open, often flowering while snow still lingers nearby.

directions: Vanguard opens silvery pearl-grey outer petals that part to reveal a soft lavender-blue interior, a two-tone effect unusual among early crocus. It is among the first tommasinianus cultivars to bloom each year, frequently flowering ahead of snowdrops finish and well before large-flowered Dutch crocus. Like other tommasinianus forms it is a superb naturalizer, seeding and multiplying freely in turf, under deciduous shrubs, and along woodland edges, and it is notably resistant to squirrel and rodent damage compared to Dutch crocus. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally before mowing any lawn planting.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun; this chrysanthus cultivar is a striking bicolor snow crocus, best sited where its rich coloring can be viewed up close.

directions: Zwanenburg Bronze produces goblet flowers with deep mahogany-bronze outer petals that open to reveal a bright golden-yellow interior, a dramatic contrast rare among the chrysanthus snow crocus. Flowers close on cloudy days and at night, opening fully only in direct sun to display the bicolor effect. Compact and early-blooming, it suits rock gardens, raised beds, or the front of a border where its detailed coloring can be appreciated at close range, and it naturalizes well in gritty, sharply drained soil.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Grand Maitre is a classic large-flowered Dutch crocus, one of the most widely planted purple cultivars for mass display.

directions: Grand Maitre bears large, silky, royal-purple goblet flowers with a faint silvery sheen at the petal base, opening wide in full sun to show bright orange stamens. As a large-flowered Dutch crocus it blooms slightly later than the species and chrysanthus types, extending the crocus season into early-to-mid spring. Its strong stems and substantial flower size make it a favorite for bold drifts in lawns, borders, and containers, and it naturalizes steadily where drainage is good.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this sieberi selection is among the earliest crocus to flower, ideal for rock gardens and troughs.

directions: Violet Queen carries deep violet-purple petals surrounding a vivid golden-yellow throat, a saturated color combination that stands out sharply against late-winter bare ground. Like the species, it is exceptionally early and cold-tolerant, often flowering through thin snow cover ahead of most other crocus. Its compact scale suits alpine troughs, scree beds, and the front of a sunny rock garden, where it multiplies gradually by offsets to form tight, long-lived clumps.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; this white sport of common grape hyacinth is a heritage cultivar dating to the 16th century, still valued for its clean color and reliable perennializing.

directions: Album is a pure white-flowered form of the common grape hyacinth, bearing the same tightly packed, urn-shaped floret spikes as the blue species but in soft ivory-white, with a light, sweet fragrance. It is one of the oldest named bulb cultivars still in cultivation, having been grown in European gardens since the 1500s, and remains just as cold-hardy and easy as the straight species. Its clean white color makes it a useful companion for blue Muscari armeniacum, Scilla, or Chionodoxa in mixed spring plantings, or for a quieter, monochrome drift on its own. Foliage emerges in fall and persists through winter; leave it undisturbed until it yellows naturally in early summer.

planting.note: Plant bulbs six weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish ahead of winter dormancy; Anna Marie is one of the most widely grown hyacinths for both garden display and indoor forcing.

directions: Anna Marie produces dense, upright spikes of soft, pale shell-pink flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening slightly earlier in the season than many other hyacinth cultivars. It is one of the most commercially popular hyacinths, prized both as a garden bulb and as an easy, reliable choice for indoor forcing in bowls or hyacinth glasses over winter. Set bulbs pointed side up about 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil, and water thoroughly after planting and again as shoots emerge in early spring. In zone 9 and warmer, pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator for 6-8 weeks before planting to ensure strong flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs six weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish ahead of winter dormancy; White Pearl is a popular pure-white hyacinth widely grown for both borders and forcing.

directions: White Pearl bears a dense, symmetrical spike of pure white, waxy florets carrying the intensely sweet fragrance typical of hyacinths, opening from pale ivory buds. It pairs cleanly with blue or purple cultivars such as Delft Blue or Peter Stuyvesant in a mixed spring bed, and its bright white color reads well in evening or shade-edge plantings. Plant bulbs pointed side up roughly 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil, and let the foliage die back completely after bloom to recharge the bulb. It is also a dependable choice for forcing indoors in pots or hyacinth glasses for midwinter bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs six weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish ahead of winter dormancy; Amsterdam is a vivid carmine-red hyacinth, one of the deepest reds available in the group.

directions: Amsterdam produces a tight, upright spike of glossy carmine-red to rose-red florets, one of the most saturated reds among widely available hyacinth cultivars, with the characteristic heavy, sweet fragrance of the species. Its bold color makes it a strong focal point in spring bulb schemes and combines well with white or pale-yellow hyacinths and early tulips for contrast. Plant bulbs pointed side up about 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, watering well at planting and again as growth resumes in spring, then allow foliage to yellow naturally after flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs six weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish ahead of winter dormancy; Peter Stuyvesant offers a deep violet-blue flower spike, richer and darker than the widely grown Delft Blue.

directions: Peter Stuyvesant carries a dense spike of deep violet-blue florets, a darker and more saturated blue-purple than the popular Delft Blue, with the strong sweet fragrance typical of the species. Its rich, near-purple tone reads dramatically against white, pale pink, or yellow hyacinths and early daffodils in a mixed spring display. Set bulbs pointed side up about 6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, watering thoroughly at planting and again as shoots emerge in early spring, then allow the foliage to die back completely before removing it.
